content: Starting and expanding health programs to achieve comprehensive coverage, both geographically and in terms of the clinical conditions managed, will be challenging if approached in a vertical manner. The renewed focus on Universal Health Coverage (UHC), strengthening Primary Health Care (PHC), and integrating the management of neglected tropical diseases (NTDs) affecting the skin offers opportunities to incorporate care for lymphedema alongside related conditions and to include hydrocele surgery within broader surgical programs. The ultimate goal is to fully integrate high-quality services for morbidity management and disability prevention (MMDP) related to lymphatic filariasis (LF) into national health systems. This will involve training healthcare staff to care for these patients, strengthening referral mechanisms from community health workers to specialists and back, and ensuring seamless service delivery. There are numerous opportunities to expand and sustain MMDP for LF, including integration with the global disability action plan, service availability and readiness assessments (SARA), promotion of UHC, and alignment with Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) 2030 as they pertain to LF and other NTDs. The global goal, as established by the WHO Expert Committee on Filarial Infections, is to achieve 100% geographic coverage with the recommended LF minimum package of care by 2030. This package includes lymphedema management, acute dermatolymphangioadenitis (ADL) treatment, and hydrocelectomy. These services should be delivered through the health system at the appropriate level and integrated with other quality health services and initiatives. To estimate the number of lymphedema and hydrocele patients, various methods are outlined in WHO guidance documents, including door-to-door surveys, population-based prevalence surveys, mass drug administration (MDA) registers, and health facility surveys. However, there is currently no gold standard methodology for patient estimation. By 2025, countries are expected to report all available data on LF morbidity, and by 2027, they should have comprehensive data on the number of lymphedema and hydrocele patients and the health facilities providing the essential package of care. The global targets for LF elimination, as part of the GPELF Strategic Plan 2021–2030, include the following: By 2023, 100% of endemic countries will report all available LF morbidity data to WHO. By 2027, 100% of endemic countries will have data for every implementation unit (IU) on the number of lymphedema and hydrocele patients and the number of health facilities providing the essential package of care. By 2025, 100% of endemic countries will include LF interventions in their UHC essential services package policy. By 2030, 100% of endemic countries will have recommended data on the quality of care provision for the minimum package of care. By 2030, 100% of endemic countries will achieve 100% geographic coverage of the LF MMDP minimum package of care. By 2030, 100% of endemic countries will provide LF interventions without out-of-pocket expenses for patients. Success will be measured by reducing human suffering associated with LF through the application of the essential package of care for people with lymphedema (or elephantiasis) and hydrocele in areas with known patients. These activities will also contribute to poverty alleviation by positively impacting the health, social, and economic status of underserved populations. National programs are encouraged to conduct situation analyses to assess the estimated number of lymphedema and hydrocele patients, the efficiency of healthcare and information systems, the policy environment, the role of advocacy, the capacity of health staff, and opportunities for integrating activities with those for other chronic diseases. This information will help identify the best service delivery platforms and models for improving access to surgery and lymphedema management training. The implementation of MMDP services should be aligned with national LF elimination plans and global goals. Countries should develop or update implementation policies and plans based on findings from situation analyses. These plans should include advocacy, social mobilization, and clear roles and responsibilities for stakeholders. The ultimate aim is to provide 100% geographic coverage for all known patients, with at least one health facility per IU offering essential lymphedema and ADL management services and the capacity to refer to higher levels of care when necessary. In areas with high disease burden or many stakeholders, a national LF committee may be established to coordinate activities, share information, and assign responsibilities. This committee should represent various sectors, including government ministries, industry, donors, non-governmental organizations, and United Nations agencies. At the peripheral level, LF committees may also be formed to involve the community and implement activities effectively.
